title.title: Schrödinger convergence at the exact Sobolev endpoint
title.subtitle: Claim: for $f \in H^{n/(2(n+1))}(\mathbb R^n)$, $e^{it\Delta}f \to f$ almost everywhere; $s = 1/3$ in the plane

plain: A quantum wave starts from a rough shape: how smooth must that shape be for the wave to return to it?

object.axisLabel: smoothness $s$ of the data $f \in H^s(\mathbb R^2)$

beats.text: How smooth must data be for the Schrödinger flow to return to it pointwise?
Below $1/3$ it can fail; strictly above, it holds. Only the endpoint was open
The claim settles the endpoint, in the plane and in every dimension

steps: Packets crossing at angles: a fixed saving, from projection theorems
Sparse packets and paired frames: bounds with no loss at all
Sum over frequencies in the right order: the endpoint holds

achievement.label: Carleson's problem at the endpoint
statement: f \in H^{\frac{n}{2(n+1)}}(\mathbb R^n) \;\Longrightarrow\; e^{it\Delta} f \to f \text{ a.e.}
achievement.context: Before: everything strictly above it (Du–Guth–Li 2017; Du–Zhang 2019)
achievement.note: Only the endpoint; the maximal estimate has $L^1$ output. 179 pages, no Lean

voice.text: How smooth must data be to return pointwise? Only the endpoint was open.

sources.quote: Bourgain's counterexample (2016) shows s ≥ n/(2(n+1)) is necessary. Du–Guth–Li (Annals 2017) proved s>1/3 in R^2
These two papers claim the endpoint itself, through a maximal estimate with $L^1$ output. That is real but narrow, and it took 179 unformalized pages.
